about: Part of the reference catalogue: designs from one published source, for testing that software reproduces them.
Jones and Nachtsheim (2011) introduce definitive screening designs: three-level designs of 2m + 1 runs for m factors,
fold-over pairs with one factor at its centre and a centre run. experiments: the six-factor design of Table 2 with its
simulated response. designs: Figure 1's designs for m = 4 to 12, with the column correlations of Table 3, the relative
efficiencies of Table 5, the powers of Table 7 and the projection counts of Table 8. Each expected item has its printed
text, where it is printed (a page and a quotation) and a check, or manual: the reason it is not recomputed.

source.title: A Class of Three-Level Designs for Definitive Screening in the Presence of Second-Order Effects
source.cite: Jones and Nachtsheim (2011), "A Class of Three-Level Designs for Definitive Screening in the Presence of Second-Order Effects", Journal of Quality Technology 43(1), 1-15
source.rights: The article is protected by copyright and is not reproduced here; read it through its DOI. This file holds facts it reports (numbers, design matrices, data) and short quotations that locate each one, for citation and for checking software. The MIT licence of process-improve does not extend to them.

The orthogonal alternatives of Table 7 are, with one centre run, the first m columns of the library's Plackett-Burman design of 2m runs for m = 6 and 10, the library's 2^(8-4) of resolution IV for m = 8, and for m = 12 the 12-run Plackett-Burman design folded over, the sign of its halves the twelfth factor (p. 11 says only 'Plackett-Burman designs'; the first twelve columns of the library's 24-run design give an average power of 0.867, and 200 random choices of twelve 0.855 to 0.894, for hypothesis 3 at |beta|/sigma = 1, where the fold-over gives the printed 0.993).

not_captured: The rows of Tables 3 and 4 for m = 13 to 20: their designs are not printed (p. 5 gives a download address at asq.org).

Table 4's caption, 'full quadratic models involving any three active factors', describes two models. Its |r_qq,ss| columns are the correlations of the estimated squares in the model of every main effect and every square, which the full quadratic model of three factors does not reproduce (0.059 for m = 6, against the printed 0.087). Its other six columns are those of the full quadratic model of one projection onto three factors, not an average over projections: every projection gives the same numbers for m = 6, 8 and 10, but for m = 7 and 12 only 14 of 35 and 130 of 220 do (x1, x2 and x3 among them), and for m = 9 and 11 the projection onto x1, x2 and x3 is not one of them (see the disagreements).

Table 8's D-efficiencies (average, minimum and maximum over the three-factor projections): they are relative to a design the paper does not name. The library's absolute D-efficiency of each projection (42.35 for each of m = 6's 20) is on another scale, but its spread agrees: every projection of m = 6, 8 and 10 has the same D-efficiency, as p. 12 says, and the largest over the smallest is 1.199, 1.079, 1.071 and 1.033 for m = 7, 9, 11 and 12, where the printed columns give 0.97/0.81, 0.95/0.88, 0.95/0.89 and 0.94/0.90.
Table 6, the six hypotheses: captured as the models and terms of Table 7's power checks, not as numbers.

Equations (4) to (6), the correlations between second-order columns as functions of m: checked where Table 3 prints them (zero for |r_qq,qs| and one constant |r_qq,st| for even m, and equation (4) at m = 4), not as formulas; the proofs of the appendix.
Figure 2 (the correlations of equations (4) and (6) for 4 to 40 factors) and Figure 3 (the column correlations of the six-factor design): plots.

Corner-point balance of the two-factor projections (p. 12): for even m each projection is a central composite design with m/2 - 1 replicates of the corners, for odd m the corners are replicated (m/2 - 1) +/- 1/2 times; a count the catalogue's check kinds do not read.

The algorithm of the paper's search (coordinate exchange from 10,000 random starting designs, pp. 4-5), and the forward stepwise and best-subset analyses of the example, beyond the AICc of the models they end with.
